stories.headline: Supreme Court: 24-hour arrest clock starts the moment police hold you
stories.question: Why does the Supreme Court say the 24-hour clock starts at detention, not arrest?
stories.dek: The Constitution lets police leave out only the travel time to court. If the clock started at a later paper arrest, police could hold people for hours with no judge watching.

so_far.text: Article 22(2) of India's Constitution says a person who is arrested must be brought before a magistrate within 24 hours. A magistrate is the judge who handles the first stage of a criminal case. Only the travel time to the court can be left out. Courts disagreed on when that clock starts. High Courts in Kerala (2025), and in Gauhati, Bombay and Punjab & Haryana (2026), said it starts the moment a person is actually held. Rulings from the Orissa, Madras and Kerala High Courts went the other way. They allowed time spent in custody before a formal arrest to be left out.

what_happened.text: On 5 November 2026 the Supreme Court settled the question. A bench of Justices Ujjal Bhuyan and Atul S Chandurkar held that the 24-hour clock starts when a person is actually detained. It does not start when police write down an arrest. The case, Sujit Das v. Union of India, came from Tripura. Police held four people during a drug search at about 2 pm on 29 September 2025. Their arrest was recorded at 11 am on 30 September. The Tripura High Court had refused them bail. The Supreme Court overturned that refusal and ordered their immediate release.

steps.text: Article 22(2) exists so that a judge, not the police, quickly decides whether a person stays locked up.
If the clock started only at formal arrest, police could hold someone for hours first, with no judge checking.
The Court called this 'buffer zone' unconstitutional. The Constitution itself leaves out only the travel time to the magistrate.
So hours spent questioning or investigating before the arrest is recorded still count against the 24 hours.
If 24 hours pass after detention without a magistrate, the person must be released, even under strict drug-law bail rules.

lesson.concept: How India's 24-hour rule after arrest works
lesson.big_idea: Once police hold someone, they have 24 hours to bring that person before a magistrate. The clock starts when the person loses their freedom. Only travel time to court is taken out.

steps.title: The rule in the Constitution
steps.text: Article 22(2) says an arrested person must be brought before a magistrate within 24 hours. A magistrate is a judge who checks whether holding that person is lawful.

steps.title: When the clock starts
steps.text: The clock starts at detention, the moment police stop you from leaving. It does not start when they write down an arrest.

steps.title: What can be taken out
steps.text: Only travel time to the magistrate's court can be subtracted. Time spent questioning or investigating before the formal arrest still counts.

steps.title: When time runs out
steps.text: If 24 hours pass after detention without a magistrate, the person must be released. Strict drug-law bail rules do not change this.

steps.title: The magistrate's check
steps.text: The magistrate must record the real time of detention. Remand can be refused if custody was unreasonably long, even under 24 hours.

apply.text: In the Tripura case, police held four people at about 2 pm on 29 September 2025 and recorded the arrest at 11 am the next day. The agency said the clock started at arrest. The Supreme Court counted from detention, rejected the buffer and freed all four.

practice.q: Meena is detained at 6 pm Friday. Her arrest is recorded at 9 am Saturday. She reaches the magistrate at 4 pm Saturday, after 2 hours of travel. Was the limit kept?
practice.answer: From detention: 6 pm Friday to 4 pm Saturday = 22 hours. Minus 2 hours of travel = 20 hours. Under 24, so the limit was kept. The magistrate must still record 6 pm as the detention time.

stories.headline: Supreme Court asks larger bench to rethink two-child poll bar
stories.question: Could the Supreme Court end two-child limits for people contesting local elections?
stories.dek: It could, but not yet. On 4 November 2026, two judges sent a 2003 ruling that upheld the limits to a larger bench. Only that bench can overturn it.

so_far.text: Some states bar people with more than two living children from panchayat posts. A panchayat is an elected village council. In July 2003, a three-judge Supreme Court bench upheld a Haryana law of this kind, in Javed v State of Haryana. It found the rule was neither arbitrary nor discriminatory, and that it served a rational purpose. The new case began with Mangala Bhimrao Ingle, a former sarpanch (village head) of Kakoda. Ingle was disqualified under Maharashtra's panchayat law after a third child. The Bombay High Court upheld that on 5 August 2025. The Supreme Court paused the High Court order on 4 November 2025.

what_happened.text: On 4 November 2026, Supreme Court Justices PS Narasimha and Alok Aradhe sent the Javed ruling to a larger bench to be reconsidered. They said two-child laws have lost relevance because fears of overpopulation have faded. Reproductive choice falls under Article 21, the right to life and personal liberty. So any limit on that choice must be tested for reasonableness. The judges said population control alone does not justify coercion. The Chief Justice of India will now set up the larger bench. No timeline was given.

steps.text: A Supreme Court bench must follow earlier rulings made by benches of the same size or larger.
Three judges decided Javed, so a two-judge bench cannot overrule it, even if it disagrees.
So the two judges wrote down their doubts and sent the question up to a larger bench.
The Chief Justice of India will form that bench. Until it rules, Javed stays binding.
If the larger bench overrules Javed, state two-child rules could face new challenges as unreasonable limits on choice.

lesson.concept: How a larger bench can overturn a past ruling
lesson.big_idea: In the Supreme Court, a bench must follow earlier rulings by benches of the same size or larger. To overturn one, judges who disagree must ask the Chief Justice for a larger bench.

steps.title: A ruling binds future cases
steps.text: When the Supreme Court decides a point of law, that decision becomes a precedent. A precedent is a rule later courts must follow. This keeps the law predictable, so people know what is allowed.

steps.title: Bench size sets the strength
steps.text: Judges sit in benches of two, three, five or more. A ruling binds every later bench of the same size or smaller. Three judges decided Javed in 2003.

steps.title: Smaller benches can only refer
steps.text: A smaller bench that doubts an earlier ruling cannot overrule it. Instead, it writes down its reasons and refers the question to a larger bench. The two-judge bench did this on 4 November 2026.

steps.title: The Chief Justice builds the bench
steps.text: The order goes to the Chief Justice of India, who decides how many judges sit on the larger bench and who they are. Until that bench rules, the old precedent still applies.

steps.title: The majority decides
steps.text: The larger bench hears arguments, and then the judges vote. If a majority agrees, the old ruling is overruled. The new view then becomes the precedent for courts across India.

practice.answer: No. Three is fewer than five, so the three-judge bench must follow the ruling. It would write down its doubts and refer the question to the Chief Justice. To overrule the ruling, the Chief Justice would need to form a bench bigger than five, say seven judges.

lesson.concept: How oil price swings reach India's import bill
lesson.big_idea: Oil prices move on expectations: news that makes supply look riskier or safer changes the price at once. For India, analysts estimated in 2025 that each $10 rise could add $13–14 billion a year to the import bill.

steps.title: Brent is the world's price tag
steps.text: Brent is a benchmark: the price of one barrel (about 159 litres) of a standard crude oil. Many oil deals around the world follow it. So when Brent moves, what India pays tends to move too.

steps.title: Prices follow expectations
steps.text: Traders buy and sell oil for delivery in the future. If news makes supply look riskier, they bid the price up before any shortage arrives. Calmer news, like hopes of peace, pulls it down.

steps.title: Hormuz is the big risk
steps.text: Iran's Revolutionary Guard calls the Strait of Hormuz closed to ships that do not coordinate with it. Tankers have hit mines there. Any hint of a new strike or a deal can change the odds traders weigh.

steps.title: Turn price into India's bill
steps.text: Analysts estimated in 2025 that each $10 rise in the average crude price could add $13–14 billion to India's yearly import bill. To use it, divide the price change by $10, then multiply by $13–14 billion.

steps.title: Averages matter, not single days
steps.text: The estimate uses the average price over a year. A one-day jump of a few per cent costs little. Prices that stay high for months cost a lot.

stories.headline: AI stock sell-off sinks S&P 500 to worst day since April 2025
stories.question: What triggered the AI stock wipeout that sank the S&P 500 on 5 November?
stories.dek: Reports blame three things: hedge funds cashing in their 2026 gains, heavy selling by small investors, and fears that Democratic wins could slow AI data-centre building. Chip stocks fell hardest, about 12%.

so_far.text: Hedge funds had built up large gains during 2026. Chipmakers such as Nvidia and AMD sell the processors that artificial intelligence (AI) data centres run on. So their shares rise and fall with hopes for AI spending. The US then held its midterm elections for Congress. Some investors feared that Democratic wins could hamper the building of AI data centres. The trading session on 5 November came straight after those elections.

what_happened.text: On 5 November 2026 the S&P 500, an index of 500 large US companies, fell 4.36% to 7,353.73. It was its worst day since April 2025. AP called it a 'wipeout for AI stocks'. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52% to 24,315, more than 10% below its high. The Dow lost 3.44%. The Philadelphia Semiconductor index, which tracks chip stocks, fell about 12%. Nvidia dropped 9.12%. All 11 S&P sectors fell. Reports summarised by CNN put the market value lost at $2.2–2.5 trillion. The VIX, a measure of how much traders expect prices to swing, jumped about 70% to 28.18.

steps.text: Hedge funds held large 2026 gains and began selling AI stocks to lock those gains in as cash.
Small investors sold heavily too. Their net selling was the heaviest since March 2020.
Investors feared that Democratic wins in Congress could slow AI data-centre building, and data centres drive chip demand.
Brent oil near $98 a barrel, on uncertainty between the US and Iran, put extra pressure on shares.
The selling spread across the whole market: all 11 S&P sectors fell, but chip stocks fell most, about 12%.

lesson.concept: How profit-taking turns into a sell-off
lesson.big_idea: A gain on a share you still hold exists only on paper until you sell. When many holders rush to lock in gains at once, prices fall, and that pushes even more holders to sell.

steps.title: Paper gain versus locked gain
steps.text: Buy a share at ₹100 and watch it rise to ₹150. Your ₹50 gain is a 'paper gain': it becomes real only when you sell. Until then, a fall in price can shrink it.

steps.title: Profit-taking means selling to lock in
steps.text: Profit-taking means selling a winning investment to turn a paper gain into cash. Reports said hedge funds did this on 5 November with their 2026 gains.

steps.title: Prices fall when sellers outnumber buyers
steps.text: A share's price is whatever the latest buyer and seller agree. When many want to sell and few want to buy, sellers must accept lower prices to find a buyer.

steps.title: Falling prices create more sellers
steps.text: As prices drop, other holders watch their paper gains shrink. Some sell to protect what is left, and that pushes prices lower again. On 5 November small investors' net selling was the heaviest since March 2020.

steps.title: Selling can spread across markets
steps.text: Once selling starts, funds may sell other shares too, to raise cash or cut risk. On 5 November all 11 S&P sectors fell, but chip stocks fell most, about 12%.

example.setup: Say a hedge fund put ₹100 crore into chip shares in January. Assume that by November the shares are worth ₹150 crore. Then, in one day, they fall 12%.

lines.label: Paper gain
lines.note: Not locked in yet; it exists only on screen.

lines.label: One-day 12% fall
lines.note: About the same size as the chip index's fall on 5 November.

lines.label: New value
lines.note: What the shares are worth after the fall.

lines.label: Gain left
lines.note: The paper gain has shrunk.

lines.label: Share of gain lost
lines.note: More than a third of the year's gain, gone in a day.

example.result: The price fell only 12%, but 36% of the year's gain disappeared. That's why funds sitting on big gains sell fast once prices turn, and their selling drags prices down further.

apply.text: That is the pattern reported on 5 November. Hedge funds sold to lock in their 2026 gains. Small investors sold heavily, and election fears hurt hopes for data-centre building. Chip shares fell about 12%, against 5.52% for the Nasdaq. Nomura's Charlie McElligott called the unwind 'wildly acute'.

practice.q: Say you bought shares for ₹1 lakh and they are now worth ₹2 lakh. They fall 10% in one day. How much gain is left?
practice.answer: Paper gain before the fall: ₹2 lakh − ₹1 lakh = ₹1 lakh. The fall: 10% of ₹2 lakh = ₹20,000. New value: ₹2,00,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹1,80,000. Gain left: ₹1,80,000 − ₹1,00,000 = ₹80,000. A 10% price fall cut your gain by a fifth.

stories.headline: Bank of England raises interest rates to 4% as inflation climbs
stories.question: Why has the Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time in three years?
stories.dek: Rising energy prices are pushing up UK prices. On 5 November 2026 the Bank of England raised its main rate to 4% to slow spending, and it signalled another rise may follow.

so_far.text: The Bank of England is the UK's central bank. Its main tool is Bank Rate, the interest rate that guides what UK banks charge borrowers and pay savers. Its job is to keep inflation, the pace at which prices rise, near a 2% target. In March 2026 its Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), the panel that sets Bank Rate, voted 9–0 to hold it at 3.75%. The MPC held the rate six times in a row. Meanwhile UK prices kept rising faster: inflation was 3.5% in the 12 months to September 2026, up from 3.1% in August.

what_happened.text: On 5 November 2026 the Bank of England raised Bank Rate by 0.25 points, from 3.75% to 4%. It was the Bank's first rise in over three years, and most analysts had expected it. The MPC voted 8–1. The one member who disagreed wanted a bigger rise, to 4.25%. Governor Andrew Bailey said rising energy prices had put enough inflationary pressure in the pipeline to justify a rise. He signalled another rise in the near future. CNBC reported that the Bank warned inflation will near 5%. AP linked the higher inflation to the Iran war.

steps.text: Energy prices have risen, and AP links the higher inflation to the Iran war.
Costlier energy spreads into many other costs, and UK inflation climbed to 3.5%, against a 2% target.
The Bank expects more pressure is still coming; CNBC reported its warning that inflation will near 5%.
A higher Bank Rate makes borrowing dearer and saving more rewarding, so people and firms spend a little less.
With less spending, sellers find it harder to raise prices, so inflation slows over the following months.

lesson.concept: How raising interest rates fights inflation
lesson.big_idea: When prices rise too fast, a central bank raises its interest rate. Borrowing gets dearer and saving pays more, so people spend less, and price rises slow down.

steps.title: The target: 2% inflation
steps.text: Inflation is how much prices rise over a year. The Bank of England aims for 2%. In September 2026 UK inflation was 3.5%, well above the target.

steps.title: Bank Rate sets money's price
steps.text: Bank Rate is the interest rate the Bank of England sets. UK banks follow it, so loans and savings get dearer or cheaper with it. On 5 November 2026 it rose from 3.75% to 4%.

steps.title: Dearer loans, less spending
steps.text: When loans cost more, families borrow and spend less, and firms delay buying. With fewer buyers, sellers find it harder to raise prices, so inflation slows.

steps.title: Compare the rate with inflation
steps.text: What matters is the interest rate minus inflation, called the real rate. If inflation is higher than the interest rate, savings lose buying power and borrowing is effectively cheap, so spending stays high.

steps.title: Act before the pressure arrives
steps.text: Rate changes take many months to work, so a central bank looks ahead. Bailey pointed to energy price pressure in the pipeline; CNBC reported the Bank warned inflation will near 5%.

example.setup: Say you keep £1,000 in a UK savings account for one year, and the account pays Bank Rate. Assume prices rise 5% over that year, close to the level CNBC reported.

lines.label: Savings at 3.75%
lines.note: The old Bank Rate.

lines.label: Basket after 5%
lines.note: What the same goods now cost.

lines.label: Gap at 3.75%
lines.note: Your savings buy less than a year ago.

lines.label: Savings at 4%
lines.note: The new Bank Rate.

lines.label: Gap at 4%
lines.note: Still a loss, but a smaller one.

example.result: The rise makes saving a little more rewarding and borrowing a little dearer, so spending cools slightly. But if inflation nears 5%, even 4% leaves savers behind, so the gap is not yet closed.

apply.text: So when energy prices pushed UK inflation to 3.5%, and the Bank saw more pressure coming, eight of nine MPC members voted to lift Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4%. That narrows the gap between interest rates and inflation. Bailey has signalled another rise, and markets expect Bank Rate near 4.75% by Christmas 2027.

practice.q: Same £1,000 at the new 4% rate, but inflation instead falls to 3.5%. Do your savings gain or lose buying power, and by how much?
practice.answer: Savings: £1,000 + 4% = £1,040. Basket: £1,000 + 3.5% = £1,035. Gap: £1,040 − £1,035 = +£5. You gain £5 of buying power, because the interest rate is now above inflation.

sections.title: World
sections.gist: France's unions held a general strike, Joshua Wong was jailed for 10 years, and Somalia's top court ordered elections within 90 days.

items.headline: France: hundreds of thousands march in nationwide general strike
items.text: On 5 November, trade unions in France held a general strike over the cost of living and cuts to public services. Hundreds of thousands of people marched in cities across the country. About 70,000 police officers were deployed for the day of demonstrations. The reports do not give an official national turnout figure. They also do not say whether unions have planned further strike days. Both are worth watching in the coming weeks.
items.background: In a general strike, trade unions call on workers in many sectors to stop work on the same day to press shared demands.
items.why: It shows how anger over prices and public service cuts is bringing large crowds onto the streets of a major European country.

items.headline: Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years
items.text: On 5 November, Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong, 30, was sentenced to 10 years in prison in a national security case. He had earlier pleaded guilty to a foreign collusion offence. The New York Times said he was accused of conspiracy to collude with foreign forces, a national security offence. Wong has been in prison since 2020. He is the only activist in Hong Kong who has been prosecuted twice under the national security law. The reports do not say whether he plans to appeal.
items.background: Hong Kong's national security law covers offences such as colluding with foreign forces. Wong is the only activist prosecuted under it twice.
items.why: A 10-year sentence for one of Hong Kong's best-known activists shows how heavily the national security law is being applied.

items.headline: Somalia's top court says president's term is over, orders elections
items.text: Somalia's Supreme Court has cancelled changes to the country's constitution, in a ruling reported on 5 November. It ruled that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's term ended on 15 May 2026. That means he has been in office for almost six months beyond his term. The court said parliament's mandate ended on 14 April 2026. Political leaders now have 30 days to agree on rules for the election. The vote itself must take place within 90 days. AFP said the ruling could bring fresh chaos to Somalia. It is not yet known whether Mohamud will accept the ruling.
items.background: Somalia's constitution had been amended. The court has now cancelled those amendments, which affects how long the president and parliament can stay in office.
items.why: The ruling sets a test of whether Somalia's leaders will follow its courts. That is the basis of stable government.

items.headline: California governor ends death sentences for all 548 inmates
items.text: California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 inmates on the state's death row, as reported on 5 November. To commute a sentence means to swap it for a lighter one. These inmates will no longer face execution. DW described the move as one of Newsom's last acts as governor. Newsom is a Democrat who is rumoured to be a possible presidential candidate. The available reports do not say what sentences replace the death penalty. They also do not say whether anyone will challenge the decision in court.
items.background: In US states, a governor can grant clemency. That is the power to reduce a sentence a court has already imposed.
items.why: Newsom's clemency removes 548 people from death row in one of America's biggest states. It has no direct effect on India.

items.headline: Bangladesh agrees to raise garment workers' minimum wage after protests
items.text: Bangladesh has agreed to raise the minimum wage for garment workers, the New York Times reported on 5 November. The decision followed protests by workers demanding higher pay. The protests shut down hundreds of garment factories in the days before the agreement. Bangladesh is the world's second-largest exporter of clothing. The reports do not give the size of the increase. They also do not say when it takes effect, or whether the protests will now end.
items.background: Garment factories are central to Bangladesh's economy. The country is the world's second-largest clothing exporter.
items.why: Pay for garment workers in India's neighbour, the world's second-largest clothing exporter, is now changing after protests closed hundreds of factories.

items.headline: Israel: 67 seats back Eisenkot; Herzog to pick on 8 November
items.text: On 5 November, Israel's President Isaac Herzog finished talks with the parties elected to the Knesset, Israel's 120-seat parliament. He said parties holding 67 seats recommended Gadi Eisenkot for prime minister, and parties with 46 seats backed Benjamin Netanyahu. Herzog plans to give one of them the mandate on Sunday, 8 November. A recommendation is not the same as joining a government. PBS reported that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor Eisenkot's won a majority. Herzog will pick whoever he thinks is likeliest to build a coalition. If neither manages it, Israel would hold a new election early in 2027.
items.background: After an Israeli election, the president consults every party. He then asks one leader to try to build a governing majority in the Knesset.
items.why: Herzog's choice decides whether Eisenkot or Netanyahu gets the first chance to form a government, or whether Israel faces another election.

sections.title: India
sections.gist: A building collapse in Old Delhi killed two, the US sanctioned Indian firms over Iranian oil, and the CBI questions the Mahadev app boss.

items.headline: Illegal building collapses in Old Delhi's Chawri Bazaar, killing two
items.text: On the morning of 5 November, a three-storey building under construction collapsed in Chawri Bazaar, Old Delhi. Two people were killed. Six fire units were sent, and the exact number of people inside was not immediately known. A senior official of the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) said the building had no approved building plan. It stood on a 50-square-metre plot, so its construction was illegal. Two MCD officials were suspended. Locals alleged that illegal building work was going on in Gali Sitara without safety measures. Many buildings nearby have been turned into warehouses and shops without any structural safety check. The area's narrow lanes slow down rescue teams.
items.background: In Delhi, the MCD must approve a building plan before construction starts. Old Delhi has crowded markets and very narrow lanes.
items.why: The collapse shows how unapproved construction and missing safety checks put lives at risk in India's crowded old city areas.

items.headline: US sanctions Indian couple and eight Indian firms over Iranian oil
items.text: The US Treasury has sanctioned India-based Suniel Kumar Sharma and his wife, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid, as reported on 5 November. It accuses them of running a network that gave false flags and shipping certificates to sanctioned vessels carrying Iranian oil. A false flag lets a ship pretend to be registered in another country. Eight India-based firms were also sanctioned, including Oceaniek Technologies India and Aryavart Ship Management. The action was taken under a US order called Executive Order 13902. The Treasury also warned the shipping industry about dealing with ships that may be falsely flagged.
items.background: The US limits sales of Iranian oil. Ships that try to get around those limits are often called a 'shadow fleet'.
items.why: Indian shipping companies that deal with falsely flagged vessels could themselves face US penalties.

items.headline: Mahadev betting app boss in CBI custody; co-founder held in UAE
items.text: Saurabh Chandrakar, accused of running the Mahadev betting app, was extradited from Oman on 1 November. Royal Oman Police had detained him using an Interpol Red Corner Notice, which is a global request to find and hold a wanted person. A Delhi court first gave the CBI two days of transit custody to bring him in. The CBI then got eight days' custody to question him. The alleged scheme is worth about ₹6,000 crore. Officials said co-promoter Ravi Uppal has been arrested in the UAE. India has started the process to bring him back. It is not yet known when the UAE will decide on that request.
items.background: The Mahadev app is accused of running an illegal betting operation in India. Its two main promoters were abroad.
items.why: Bringing both promoters back would let Indian investigators pursue a case worth about ₹6,000 crore.

items.headline: India in final-stage talks to sell more missiles to the Philippines
items.text: On 5 November Reuters reported, citing sources, that India is in the final stage of talks to expand its missile sale to the Philippines. The report available here does not say which missile systems are involved. It also does not give the deal's value or a date for signing. It is not yet known when, or whether, an agreement will be announced.
items.background: India already sells missiles to the Philippines. These talks are about expanding that sale.
items.why: A bigger order would grow India's defence exports and its security ties with a Southeast Asian partner.

items.headline: India to make state power companies add energy storage
items.text: Power Secretary Pankaj Agarwal told the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit that India will soon require state-owned power utilities to add energy storage. This was reported on 5 November, and no deadline was given. In September, India curtailed up to 118.6 GW of solar and wind capacity, according to JMK Research. That means producers were told to cut output because demand did not match supply and power lines were full. The government has approved ₹14,500 crore to help pay for 92 GWh of grid-scale storage. That is 30 GWh of batteries, 60 GWh of pumped storage and 2 GWh of newer technologies. From July 2027, solar and wind developers would need batteries on site.
items.background: Solar and wind power rise and fall with the weather. Storage holds spare power and releases it when demand is high.
items.why: More storage means less clean power is wasted. That helps India rely more on solar and wind.

sections.gist: A new visa rule for some refugees, Delhi's air stuck at 'very poor', and TRAI backs phones linking straight to satellites.

items.headline: Home Ministry now requires visas for some undocumented refugees
items.text: The Home Ministry has changed a rule, The Hindu reported on 5 November. The change covers members of six non-Muslim communities from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan who entered India before 31 December 2024. It applies to people who came because they feared "religious persecution", meaning harm because of their faith. Some came without valid travel documents. Others had papers that have since expired. These people now need a visa, which is official permission to stay in India. The report does not say how or by when they must apply. It is also not yet known how many people this affects.
items.background: Some people from three neighbouring countries entered India without valid papers, saying they fled persecution over their religion. Until now, their legal status here was unsettled.
items.why: It changes the paperwork rules for a group of refugees living in India. Families affected need to watch for application steps.

items.headline: Delhi air stays 'very poor' as firework curbs begin
items.text: Delhi's air quality index (AQI) was 369 on 4 November. The AQI is one number that sums up how polluted the air is; higher is worse. It was the third straight day in the 'very poor' band, ahead of Diwali. Authorities brought in GRAP-II across the capital. GRAP is Delhi's step-by-step pollution plan, and each stage adds stricter limits as air gets worse. Rules limiting fireworks also came into force, the BBC reported. Watch whether the AQI crosses into a worse band around Diwali. If it does, the next GRAP stage would add more limits.
items.background: Delhi's air usually gets worse in early winter. The city uses a staged action plan, GRAP, that tightens rules as pollution rises.
items.why: Millions in Delhi breathe this air. GRAP stages and firework curbs change what residents and businesses may do.

items.headline: TRAI backs phones that connect straight to satellites
items.text: On 5 November TRAI, India's telecom regulator, proposed new rules for satellite networks. It wants a separate licence category for companies that run satellite communication networks. Licences would last 20 years. Companies would pay 8% of their revenue as a fee. That means ₹8 on every ₹100 they earn. TRAI also backed 'direct-to-device' service. This lets an ordinary phone connect straight to a satellite, with no mobile tower in between. These are proposals, not final rules. It is not yet known when the government will decide on them, or when such services could start.
items.background: TRAI advises the government on telecom rules. Satellites can reach places where mobile towers are hard or costly to build.
items.why: Direct-to-device service could one day give phone signal in remote areas. Final rules will set costs for satellite firms.

sections.title: Markets & money
sections.gist: The Sensex rose for a sixth straight day, SEBI eased mutual fund settlement and cleared Mahanadi Coalfields' IPO, and Adani Ports agreed to buy Evos.

items.headline: Sensex jumps 2,009 points, its sixth gain in a row
items.text: On 5 November the Sensex rose 2,008.61 points, or 2.60%, to close at 79,310.01. It was the index's sixth straight day of gains. The Nifty 50 rose 576 points, or 2.40%, to 24,536.60. That is its highest level in three months. To feel the size: ₹1 lakh tracking the Sensex would have gained about ₹2,600 in one day. The reports used here do not explain what drove the rise. Watch whether the run of gains holds in the next trading sessions.
items.background: The Sensex tracks 30 large companies on the BSE. The Nifty 50 tracks 50 large companies on the NSE.
items.why: Many Indians hold these shares through mutual funds and pension savings, so big index moves change portfolio values.

items.headline: SEBI clears IPO of Coal India unit Mahanadi Coalfields
items.text: SEBI has approved the IPO of Mahanadi Coalfields, a unit of Coal India, Reuters reported on 5 November. An IPO is when a company first sells shares to the public. This one is an 'offer for sale': Coal India sells existing shares, so the money goes to Coal India, not to Mahanadi Coalfields. Coal India will sell 66.18 crore shares. That is 10% of the company, Rediff reported. So Coal India would still own most of it. The price, total size and opening date have not yet been reported.
items.background: Coal India is a large state-owned coal miner. Mahanadi Coalfields is one of its subsidiary companies.
items.why: It gives ordinary investors a chance to buy into a Coal India unit once the issue opens.

items.headline: Adani Ports to buy Dutch storage firm Evos for €2.56 billion
items.text: On 5 November Adani Ports agreed to buy Evos, a Dutch company that stores liquids such as fuels and chemicals. The all-cash deal is valued at €2.56 billion; Reuters put it at $2.88 billion. All-cash means Adani pays money, not its own shares. Adani gets eight terminals in Europe. Together they can store 6.3 million cubic metres, or 6.3 billion litres. The terminals are in the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp region, Hamburg and the Mediterranean. These are major energy and industrial hubs. When the deal will close, and how the cash will be raised, has not been reported.
items.background: Adani Ports runs ports in India. Liquid cargo terminals are big tank farms where ships unload fuels and chemicals.
items.why: It is a large overseas purchase by an Indian company, moving Adani Ports into Europe's main energy hubs.

sections.title: Tech & AI
sections.gist: US voters rejected local AI data centres, Anthropic's IPO filing showed huge commitments, and Nvidia chips waited in Hong Kong for Beijing's approval.

items.headline: US voters reject AI data centres in local ballot votes
items.text: On 3 November US voters decided many local questions on data centres. These are large buildings full of computers that run AI. Ballotpedia counted 41 such ballot measures across 10 states. Ohio alone had 21, about half of them. Tom's Hardware counted 45 measures. It reported that Americans voted against the projects by a wide margin. The two counts differ, and the full results have not been tallied here. Watch whether AI companies change where they build. There is no direct effect on readers in India.
items.background: AI companies need huge data centres. Many need local approval, and some US towns put that choice to a public vote.
items.why: Local resistance can slow where and how fast the AI industry can build the computers it needs.

items.headline: Anthropic IPO filing shows $895 billion in spending commitments
items.text: Anthropic, the AI company, has filed an amended document for its IPO. An IPO is a company's first sale of shares to the public. The filing shows about $17 billion of revenue in a quarter, which is three months. It also shows about $895 billion of commitments to buy or lease things, such as computing power. That is more than 50 times its quarterly revenue. On 4 November Seeking Alpha said the IPO is expected to value Anthropic at $1.5 trillion, under the ticker ANT. The listing date has not been reported.
items.background: Anthropic builds AI models. Training and running them needs vast computing power, which companies often commit to buy years ahead.
items.why: It is one of the biggest tests of whether investors will pay for AI firms' huge spending plans.

items.headline: 600,000 Nvidia AI chips wait in Hong Kong for China's approval
items.text: About 600,000 Nvidia H200 chips are sitting in Hong Kong, Reuters reported on 5 November, citing sources. They are waiting to be shipped to mainland China. The hold-up is in Beijing. China's government has not given approval for large-scale imports of the chips. Without it, the chips cannot move in bulk. It is not yet known when, or whether, Beijing will approve them. It is also not known why Beijing is holding back.
items.background: Nvidia's H200 is an advanced chip used to train and run AI models. Sales to China depend on government approvals.
items.why: It shows governments, not only companies, now decide where advanced AI chips can go.

items.headline: Hackers hit freezers storing blood at French blood service
items.text: Freezers that store blood in France were affected by a cyberattack, the BBC reported on 4 November. Modern freezers are often linked to the internet so staff can watch them. That link can let attackers in. CBS News said the attack came days after other freezer hacks in Europe. Those earlier hacks also hit supermarkets. There are several theories about who did it, but no one has been confirmed as responsible. It is not yet known how much blood, if any, was lost.
items.background: Many everyday machines, including freezers, now connect to the internet. That makes them possible targets for hackers.
items.why: Attacks on equipment like blood freezers can put health and food supplies at risk, not just data.

items.headline: Google to put another $15 billion into Malaysian data centres
items.text: On 4 November Google said it will invest US$15 billion in Malaysia in 2027 and 2028. The money will expand its data centres there. Data centres are buildings full of computers that run online services and AI. The sum works out to about US$7.5 billion a year. Malay Mail reported this is an additional commitment. It said the investment would support 37,000 jobs. Watch for where in Malaysia the new capacity is built and when it opens.
items.background: Big tech firms are building data centres across Asia to run AI and cloud services close to users.
items.why: It shows how much money is flowing into Asian data centres as countries compete to host AI computing.

sections.title: Science, health & climate
sections.gist: A UN report finds a big shortfall in climate adaptation money before COP31. Also: US measles at a 30-year high, and NASA's Swift telescope falls.

items.headline: UN report: poorer countries get about a tenth of adaptation money they need
items.text: On 4 November the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) released its Adaptation Gap Report 2026. Adaptation means preparing for climate harm, like building sea walls or growing heat-proof crops. UNEP says developing countries will need about $305 billion a year by 2035. In 2024 they received $28.2–31.7 billion in international public money. That was up only about $1 billion from 2023. So they get roughly one dollar for every ten they need. COP30 set a goal of tripling this money by 2035. Even that would cover only about 20–29% of needs. The next UN climate summit, COP31, runs in Antalya, Türkiye, from 9 to 20 November 2026.
items.background: Rich countries have promised money to help poorer countries cope with climate damage. Each yearly UN climate summit (a 'COP') argues over how much.
items.why: India is a developing country facing heatwaves and floods. How much adaptation money COP31 promises affects funds that countries like India can seek.

items.headline: Ancient DNA suggests Germanic arrived in Scandinavia later than thought
items.text: Two studies in the journal Nature used ancient DNA to trace where the Germanic and Celtic languages came from. The researchers described the work on 4 November. They studied DNA from thousands of prehistoric Europeans, including more than 700 people sequenced for the first time. The authors suggest the early form of Germanic reached Scandinavia about 4,000 years ago. It came with a second group of people with steppe ancestry. That is roughly 800 years later than scholars traditionally assumed. For Celtic, the genetic evidence best fits an origin in Central Europe, linked to the Urnfield culture.
items.background: Languages leave no bones, but people who speak them move. Tracking ancient people's DNA can show which migrations likely carried a language.
items.why: Germanic and Celtic belong to the same Indo-European family as Hindi and Bengali, so these methods also inform debates about India's language history.

items.headline: Pennsylvania reports sixth measles death as US has worst year since 1990s
items.text: On 4 November Pennsylvania's Department of Health confirmed its sixth measles-linked death. The person lived in Jefferson County and was not vaccinated. Pennsylvania has 1,467 confirmed cases this year, up 77 in seven days. Of those, 283 needed hospital care, about one patient in five. Only five patients, under 1% of cases, had been vaccinated. Across the US, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) counted 4,852 confirmed cases as of 29 October. That makes 2026 the worst US measles year since the early 1990s.
items.background: Measles is a highly contagious virus. Two vaccine doses prevent it, so outbreaks grow where many people skip vaccination.
items.why: No direct effect on India. It shows how quickly measles returns when vaccination rates fall, even in a rich country.

items.headline: NASA's Swift telescope burns up over Sumatra after 22 years
items.text: NASA's Swift Observatory fell back into the atmosphere at 6:09 p.m. IST on 4 November, over North Sumatra, Indonesia. The US Space Force confirmed it. Swift had worked for nearly 22 years. It watched for gamma-ray bursts, the brightest flashes of energy in the universe, often from dying or colliding stars. Over its life it recorded more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and 1,400 exploding stars. A private company, Katalyst, tried to rescue it with its LINK spacecraft, but the attempt failed.
items.background: Satellites in low orbit slowly lose height because of thin air drag. Without a boost, they eventually fall and burn up.
items.why: The failed rescue tested whether private spacecraft can extend the life of ageing satellites, a growing business worldwide.

sections.title: Formula 1
sections.gist: 1980 champion Alan Jones dies at 80. In Brazil, Haas drops Ocon for debutant Camara and McLaren brings new parts.

items.headline: Alan Jones, 1980 F1 champion and Williams' first title winner, dies at 80
items.text: Alan Jones, the 1980 Formula 1 world champion, died aged 80 on the Gold Coast in Australia. His wife, Amanda Butler-Davis, said in a family statement that he died after a short illness. The announcement came on 5 November. Jones was the first Williams driver to win the title, and the last Australian to do so. He won 11 grands prix. His last win came in 1981. He then surprised the sport by quitting at the end of 1981. That opened a seat for Keke Rosberg, who won the 1982 title with Williams. Williams called Jones 'a true Australian icon and a Williams legend'.
items.background: Williams is one of F1's oldest teams. Jones's 1980 title was its first, starting a run of championship success.
items.why: His title made Williams a winning team, and his sudden exit shaped who won the next championship.

items.headline: Brazil GP: Haas drops Ocon, Camara debuts, McLaren tests 2027 parts
items.text: Haas has dropped Esteban Ocon for good. Brazilian Rafael Camara, already due to race for Haas in 2027, makes his F1 debut at his home race at Interlagos. He replaces Ryo Hirakawa, who stood in for Ocon in Mexico. In Friday practice on 6 November, Cadillac test driver Colton Herta drives Sergio Perez's car. It is his sixth practice outing this season. He needs one more point to reach the 40 required for a superlicence, the FIA permit to race in F1. McLaren brings new front and rear wings and floor parts. Its aerodynamics chief Peter Prodromou says the front-wing idea will carry into the 2027 car. Lando Norris is unsure the parts will fix what he calls a 'horrible' car.
items.background: Haas first benched Ocon for the Mexico race, using Hirakawa instead. Brazil confirms the break is permanent.
items.why: Haas is moving to its 2027 line-up early, and Herta is one point from being eligible to race in F1.

sections.title: Cricket — the masala
sections.gist: CSK sign Livingstone at less than half his old fee in a trade with SRH. The first Sri Lanka ODI moves from Delhi.

items.headline: CSK get Livingstone from SRH, at less than half his old fee
items.text: On 5 November, Chennai Super Kings (CSK) and Sunrisers Hyderabad (SRH) agreed a four-player trade ahead of the IPL 2027 auction. Khaleel Ahmed and Nathan Ellis move from CSK to SRH. Liam Livingstone and Jack Edwards move from SRH to CSK. The money story is Livingstone. SRH bought him for ₹13 crore at the 2026 auction. He joins CSK on ₹6 crore, a pay cut of ₹7 crore, so his new fee is less than half the old one. Edwards stays at ₹3 crore. The reports do not give the date of the IPL 2027 auction.
items.background: Before an IPL auction, teams can swap players with each other. At the auction, franchises then bid for the players still available.
items.why: Two IPL sides have reshaped their squads before the 2027 auction, and a big-money signing has moved on a much smaller contract.

items.headline: India–Sri Lanka first ODI moved from Delhi to Visakhapatnam
items.text: On 5 November, the first India–Sri Lanka ODI was moved from Delhi to Visakhapatnam. The change came at the request of the DDCA, Delhi's cricket association. It cited planned renovation work at the stadium and possible weather disruption. The Hindu reported that even without the outfield renovation at Arun Jaitley Stadium, Delhi's poor air in December would have been a major problem for the match. Sri Lanka will play three ODIs and three T20Is in India, with the tour starting on 13 December.
items.background: The DDCA runs cricket in Delhi, and Delhi's matches are played at the Arun Jaitley Stadium. Its outfield is due to be renovated.
items.why: Delhi's poor air in December is now a real factor in deciding where India's home matches can be played.

quiz.q: Police hold a man at 8 am, record his arrest at 8 pm, and bring him to court at 11 am the next day. The journey took 1 hour. Was the limit kept?
options: Yes, only 15 hours passed after the arrest was recorded
No, 26 hours passed after detention, even after removing travel time
Yes, time spent questioning before arrest does not count
quiz.why: The clock starts at detention (8 am). Twenty-seven hours minus one hour of travel leaves 26, which is over 24.

quiz.q: Why couldn't Justices Narasimha and Aradhe simply overrule Javed themselves?
options: Three judges decided Javed, and that binds any smaller bench
Only Parliament can overrule a Supreme Court ruling
The states asked the court not to decide the matter
quiz.why: A bench must follow rulings by benches of the same size or larger. So a two-judge bench can only refer a three-judge ruling upward.

quiz.q: Brent fell about 9% after the US vote, yet Iran still calls Hormuz closed. What does that suggest?
options: Traders were pricing changed expectations about future risk, not a reopened strait
The strait reopened to all ships on 4 November
Mine strikes on tankers stopped after the election
quiz.why: Prices react to the odds of future trouble. The strait was still called closed, and mines hit tankers on 4 and 5 November.
